expectedText:
TEMPORARY (PENDENTE LITE) SPOUSAL SUPPORT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · John Doe

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Temporary (Pendente Lite) Spousal Support Information Sheet concerns Jane Doe and John Doe, who were married on June 1, 2010 and separated on January 1, 2026, in connection with a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, legal separation, or nullity filed or to be filed in the California superior court for Los Angeles County. It describes California's statutory authority for a court to order spousal support while such a proceeding is pending, before any final judgment, and how that authority and its governing standard differ from the post-judgment spousal-support standard addressed elsewhere in this corpus's Marital Settlement Agreement document. It is not itself a request for order, notice of motion, declaration, or court order, and completing it does not create, modify, or terminate any temporary spousal support obligation between Jane Doe and John Doe. Only a court order, applying the statutes described here to the facts of an actual pending proceeding, can do that.

COURT'S AUTHORITY TO ORDER SUPPORT WHILE A PROCEEDING IS PENDING
California's Family Code authorizes a court to order support during the pendency of a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties, during the pendency of a proceeding under the state's child-custody provisions, or in any proceeding where the support of a minor child (or a child for whom support is otherwise authorized) is at issue. On that authority, the court may order either spouse to pay any amount necessary for the support of the other spouse, subject to a statutory cross-reference addressed separately in this document, and may separately order either or both parents to pay any amount necessary for the support of a child. This authority for a support order during the pendency of the case is distinct from, and does not depend on, a final judgment of dissolution, legal separation, or nullity; it is commonly referred to as "temporary" or "pendente lite" support because it operates only while the underlying proceeding remains pending.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "During the pendency of any proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties or under Division 8 (commencing with Section 3000) (custody of children) or in any proceeding where there is at issue the support of a minor child or a child for whom support is authorized under Section 3901 or 3910, the court may order (a) either spouse to pay any amount that is necessary for the support of the other spouse, consistent with the requirements of subdivisions (i) and (m) of Section 4320 and Section 4325, or (b) either or both parents to pay any amount necessary for the support of the child, as the case may be."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3600 (California Legislative Information text), the court's authority to order spousal and child support during the pendency of a proceeding (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3600.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 3600); no additional independent source was found for this. The same section also authorizes support orders for a minor child (the clause of the quoted text beginning "or (b)"); that child-support authority is not the subject of this document, which addresses only the spousal-support half of the section. Section 3600 sits in Family Code Division 9, Part 1, Chapter 4 ("Spousal and Child Support During Pendency of Proceeding," §§ 3600-3604) — a correction from an initial assumption that the chapter ran only through § 3603; it in fact runs through § 3604, and an adjoining section in that same chapter, § 3601, was reviewed but not used here because it addresses only when a child-support order (not a spousal-support order) terminates by operation of law. This document does not address every type of proceeding referenced in § 3600 (for example, a standalone custody proceeding under Division 8, or a proceeding concerning a child for whom support is authorized under Sections 3901 or 3910); it focuses on support pending a dissolution, legal-separation, or nullity proceeding between spouses.

HOW THE TEMPORARY-SUPPORT STANDARD DIFFERS FROM THE POST-JUDGMENT STANDARD
When a court orders temporary spousal support under this pendency authority, the statute does not require the court to weigh the full, multi-factor list of circumstances that governs a post-judgment spousal-support order. Instead, the statute requires only that a temporary spousal-support order be consistent with two specific subdivisions of that post-judgment factor list — the history-of-domestic-violence factor and the abusive-spouse-conviction factor — together with a separate statute addressing a domestic-violence-related misdemeanor conviction. The domestic-violence-history factor directs consideration of all documented evidence of any history of domestic violence between the parties, including matters such as a plea of nolo contendere, emotional distress from domestic violence, a prior protective order, or a court's finding of domestic violence during the pendency of certain proceedings. The abusive-spouse-conviction factor separately provides that the criminal conviction of an abusive spouse must be considered toward a reduction or elimination of a spousal support award. The cross-referenced separate statute establishes a rebuttable presumption that, where one spouse has certain domestic-violence-related misdemeanor convictions against the other spouse, an award of spousal support to the convicted spouse from the injured spouse is prohibited. Outside of these specific cross-references, the statutory text examined for this document does not itself list the broader set of factors — such as the marital standard of living, each party's earning capacity, or the duration of the marriage — that governs a final, post-judgment spousal-support order under a separate part of the Family Code.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "During the pendency of any proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties or under Division 8 (commencing with Section 3000) (custody of children) or in any proceeding where there is at issue the support of a minor child or a child for whom support is authorized under Section 3901 or 3910, the court may order (a) either spouse to pay any amount that is necessary for the support of the other spouse, consistent with the requirements of subdivisions (i) and (m) of Section 4320 and Section 4325"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3600 (California Legislative Information text), the cross-reference tying temporary spousal support to Section 4320, subdivisions (i) and (m), and Section 4325 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3600.)
  "(i) All documented evidence of any history of domestic violence, as defined in Section 6211, between the parties or perpetrated by either party against either party’s child, including, but not limited to, consideration of: (1) A plea of nolo contendere. (2) Emotional distress resulting from domestic violence perpetrated against the supported party by the supporting party. (3) Any history of violence against the supporting party by the supported party. (4) Issuance of a protective order after a hearing pursuant to Section 6340. (5) A finding by a court during the pendency of a divorce, separation, or child custody proceeding, or other proceeding under Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200), that the spouse has committed domestic violence."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4320(i) (California Legislative Information text), the domestic-violence-history factor cross-referenced by Section 3600 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4320.)
  "(m) The criminal conviction of an abusive spouse shall be considered in making a reduction or elimination of a spousal support award in accordance with Section 4324.5 or 4325."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4320(m) (California Legislative Information text), the abusive-spouse-conviction factor cross-referenced by Section 3600 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4320.)
  "(a) In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage where there is a criminal conviction for a domestic violence misdemeanor or a criminal conviction for a misdemeanor that results in a term of probation pursuant to Section 1203.097 of the Penal Code perpetrated by one spouse against the other spouse entered by the court within five years prior to the filing of the dissolution proceeding or during the course of the dissolution proceeding, there shall be a rebuttable presumption that the following shall apply: (1) An award of spousal support to the convicted spouse from the injured spouse is prohibited."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4325(a)-(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), the domestic-violence-misdemeanor-conviction presumption cross-referenced by Section 3600 and Section 4320(m) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4325.)
  Known gap: Family Code § 4320(i) and § 4320(m) are two non-contiguous subdivisions of the same statutory section; they are quoted below as two separate citation entries rather than stitched together with an ellipsis. Family Code § 3600 and § 4325 are each independent statutory sections, not subdivisions of § 4320. This document does not reproduce or address the remaining lettered subdivisions of § 4320 (for example, marketable skills, standard of living, or duration of the marriage) that govern a post-judgment support order — those are addressed in this corpus's Marital Settlement Agreement document. This document also does not independently fetch or verify Family Code § 4324.5, which § 4320(m) cross-references alongside § 4325. Separately, on the question of any local-court guideline-formula practice for temporary spousal support: the statutory sections fetched for this document (§§ 3600, 4320(i), 4320(m), 4325) contain no reference to a computerized or numeric guideline formula for temporary spousal support. That is a real difference from child support, where a separate statute (Family Code § 4055, cited and quoted in this corpus's Child Support Agreement document) codifies a guideline formula in the statute itself. Because no comparable formula language appears in the temporary-spousal-support provisions verified here, this document does not describe or endorse any specific county's local-rule guideline-formula practice (sometimes used by California courts to compute a proposed temporary spousal support figure) — that practice, if any, rests on local court rule rather than on the statutory sections this document verifies, and this document takes no position on which counties use it or how any such formula is calculated.

AUTOMATIC UNENFORCEABILITY DURING A PERIOD OF RECONCILIATION
Unless the support order itself specifies otherwise, an order for spousal or child support made under this pendency authority is not enforceable during any period in which the parties have reconciled and are living together. This reconciliation-based unenforceability operates by statute rather than by separate court order; it applies unless the order's own terms provide differently.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Unless the order specifies otherwise, an order made pursuant to this chapter is not enforceable during any period in which the parties have reconciled and are living together."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3602 (California Legislative Information text), the reconciliation-based unenforceability of a temporary support order (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3602.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 3602); no additional independent source was found for this. The statute does not itself define "reconciled" or specify what evidence establishes that the parties are "living together" for this purpose, and it does not state whether or how a party must raise this unenforceability in order to rely on it. This document does not address how a court or the parties determine, in a particular case, whether either condition is met.

MODIFICATION, TERMINATION, AND THE LIMIT ON RETROACTIVITY
An order for spousal or child support made under this pendency authority may be modified or terminated at any time while the underlying proceeding remains pending, except as to any amount that already accrued before the date the modifying or terminating party filed the notice of motion or order to show cause. Separately, an order made under this pendency authority does not prejudice either party's rights, or a child's rights, with respect to any subsequent order the court may make in the same proceeding — for example, a final, post-judgment support order entered later in the case.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An order made pursuant to this chapter may be modified or terminated at any time except as to an amount that accrued before the date of the filing of the notice of motion or order to show cause to modify or terminate."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3603 (California Legislative Information text), modification or termination of a temporary support order, and the bar on retroactive modification (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3603.)
  "An order made pursuant to this chapter does not prejudice the rights of the parties or the child with respect to any subsequent order which may be made."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3604 (California Legislative Information text), the non-prejudice effect of a temporary support order on later orders (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3604.)
  Known gap: § 3603 and § 3604 are independent statutory sections within the same chapter (Chapter 4, §§ 3600-3604), not subdivisions of a single section. Neither section specifies what showing, if any, a party must make to obtain a modification or termination of a temporary support order, or otherwise states the standard a court applies in deciding whether to grant one; this document does not address that standard. This document also does not address how or whether a temporary support order automatically terminates upon entry of a final judgment of dissolution or legal separation, beyond the non-prejudice principle stated in § 3604 — that question was not independently researched for this document.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — NOT A COURT FILING
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on January 1, 2026 at Los Angeles, California.

Signature of Jane Doe: ☐ _________________________
